sources.citation: Wurm, Stephen A. 2007. Australasia and the Pacific. In Christopher Moseley (ed.), Encyclopedia of the World's Endangered Languages, 425-577. London: Routledge. Entry 'Kaningara (or Kaningra) [103]', p. 500 (with the cross-referenced structural notes in the 'Ak' entry, pp. 469-470, and 'Damal' entry).
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: Kaningara entry: 'The Sepik Hill languages have SERP structural features (see the Ak entry), but have been influenced in their structure by TNGP languages and show some TNGP features (for those see the Damal entry).' Ak entry (generic SERP profile): 'It corresponds largely to the usual SERP structural characteristics; the languages are very rarely tonal. Morphological complexity is low to medium..'. Damal entry lists 'phonologically relevant tones in many of them' as a TNGP feature. Nothing about word stress; no Kaningara data. Extract (entries only). the full scanned file was not retained.

sources.citation: Pawley, Andrew, Robert Attenborough, Jack Golson & Robin Hide (eds.) 2005. Papuan Pasts: Cultural, Linguistic and Biological Histories of Papuan-speaking Peoples. sources.note: No Kaningra linguistic data anywhere in the volume (a full-text search for stress/accent the 14 MB PDF; file not kept).

sources.citation: Bruce, Les. 1984. The Alamblak language of Papua New Guinea (East Sepik). Pacific Linguistics C-81. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Alamblak only; the text never mentions Kaningra/Kaningara (a full-text search for stress/accent the full text). Not usable for Kaningra.

sources.citation: Bruce, Leslie P. 1979. A grammar of Alamblak (Papua New Guinea). PhD thesis, ANU. Comparative Sepik Hill appendix pp. 472-519 (Kaningara cognate figures, one prenasalised form nganT 'banana', negator kaha).
sources.note: Nothing about Kaningara stress; the appendix is lexicostatistic and sound-correspondence work built on Dye et al. 1968 data (Kaningara shares 46%/44% cognates with Alamblak/Sumariup; 27% of items non-cognate with any Sepik Hill language). No stress/accent/tone remark anywhere after p. 472.

sources.citation: Bruce, Leslie P., Jr. 1975. Alamblak alveopalatals - dead portmanteaus. In R. Conrad, W. Dye, N. Thomson & L. Bruce Jr., Papers in New Guinea Linguistics No. 18, 91-102. Pacific Linguistics A-40. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Only an Alamblak transcription convention (p. 101): 'Non-phonemic stress ['] is indicated immediately preceding the stressed syllable. Raised vowel symbols.. indicate non-syllabicity. (See Bruce, 1974.)' -- applies to the Karawari/Kuvenmas Alamblak forms in Table 2. Nothing on Kaningara stress or tone; a full-text search for stress/accent the text for stress/tone/tonal/accent/pitch finds only this line.

sources.citation: Laycock, Donald C. & John Z'graggen. 1975. The Sepik-Ramu Phylum. In S. A. Wurm (ed.), New Guinea Area Languages and Language Study, vol. 1: Papuan Languages and the New Guinea Linguistic Scene, 731-763. Pacific Linguistics C-38. Canberra: ANU.
sources.note: Phylum-wide feature list (p. 731-732) includes 'lack of complex suprasegmental systems' and low vowel inventories with a quasi-phonemic schwa; the Sepik Hill section says only that few publications exist (SIL teams in Alamblak, Bahinemo, Sanio, Hewa). The only tonal discussion concerns Abau/Iwam (Upper Sepik). No stress statement for any Sepik Hill language.

sources.citation: Laycock, Donald C. 1973. Sepik languages: checklist and preliminary classification. Pacific Linguistics B-25. Canberra: ANU. Entry no. 95 KANINGRA, p. 29 (p. 33).
sources.note: Nothing. The whole entry is: 'Villages: Kaningara, Yamondindei [CD 39E]. Comments: Basel list; all other data, except population, from Dye and Townsends (1969).' No phonological remark for Kaningra; a full-text search for stress/accent in the book finds no Kaningra material.

sources.citation: Dye, Wayne, Patricia Townsend & William Townsend. 1969 [1968]. The Sepik Hill languages: a preliminary report. Oceania 39(2): 146-156.
sources.note: The catalog has no record for Kaningra and no existing statements; this work adds nothing on stress. It is the only published primary data on Kaningra (327 speakers, Kaningra and Yamandenai villages on the Blackwater River; word list recorded at Kaningra village, p. 147), but the Kaningra word list itself is not printed (Table 2 gives only Alamblak, Kapriman, Bahinemo, Sanio, pp. 151-152); Kaningra appears only as a row in the consonant-correspondence table (p. 149) and the cognate-percentage table (p. 153). The orthography footnote lists consonant symbols only, no stress or tone marks. scann…
